analysis.one_liner: Delays the health reform law's rollout until the Supreme Court rules on the individual mandate.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to eight House committees, never got a hearing or a vote in any of them, and died when the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have frozen every part of the Affordable Care Act that had not yet taken effect — including the 2014 coverage expansions — until the Supreme Court issued a ruling on whether the law's individual mandate is constitutional. It also barred the federal government from writing any implementing regulations or preparing to launch the law's remaining provisions in the meantime [S2] [S3]. Because the timing of a Supreme Court decision could not be controlled, the freeze could have lasted an unknown period even if the Court ultimately upheld the law [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the immediate winners would have been people and employers who would otherwise bear the law's costs: higher-income taxpayers who help fund the law's coverage subsidies, and larger employers facing the employer coverage requirement, who would have gotten an open-ended reprieve [S3]. States that had sued over the mandate would also have gained leverage [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers and higher-income taxpayers facing ACA costs

how_it_helps.text: It suspends every provision of the ACA and the health-related provisions of the 2010 reconciliation law that were not yet in effect, so requirements that had not kicked in would not kick in until a Supreme Court ruling [S2] [S3].
It prohibits the federal government from issuing further regulations or taking any other steps to implement the law during the freeze [S2] [S3].
The delay was conditioned on pending lawsuits: the freeze would lift only when the Supreme Court ruled on the constitutionality of the requirement to maintain minimum essential coverage [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Uninsured Americans and people with pre-existing conditions would keep waiting for the law's not-yet-effective benefits — the Medicaid expansion, premium subsidies, and the ban on denying coverage for pre-existing conditions. Insurers and state officials who had already begun building to the law's deadlines would also have faced uncertainty about whether to keep preparing [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Uninsured people waiting for coverage and protections

drawbacks.text: The delay had no set end date: it would last until the Supreme Court ruled, and even a ruling upholding the law would have come only after the government was barred from writing rules or preparing in the meantime, pushing back the date millions of uninsured people could get coverage [S2] [S3].

Parts of the law had already taken effect and were being phased in; freezing the remainder would have left insurers, states, and consumers mid-transition in limbo, unsure whether to keep building toward deadlines that could be pushed back indefinitely [S3].
The bill did not fix or replace anything in the law; it simply stopped its remaining provisions, so its practical effect was to delay help for uninsured people without offering any alternative [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For opponents of the law, the bill offered a constitutionally principled pause pending the courts. For ordinary people, the cost was concrete: the 2014 coverage expansions — Medicaid expansion, premium subsidies, and guaranteed coverage regardless of pre-existing conditions — would have been pushed back by an unknown amount, with no preparation allowed even to be ready if the Court upheld the law. The freeze would have fallen entirely on people waiting for coverage, while employers and higher-income taxpayers facing the law's costs gained time.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to eight House committees at once and never got a hearing or a vote in any of them; it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Representative Kevin Brady of Texas, joined by Tom Graves of Georgia, introduced the bill on February 11, 2011 [S3] [S5].

The Speaker referred it to eight committees at once — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, Natural Resources, Judiciary, Rules, Appropriations, and House Administration [S5].
Within weeks it was further referred to subcommittees — including the Health and Constitution subcommittees — but none of the eight committees or their subcommittees ever took it up [S5].
Fourteen Republicans cosponsored the bill and no Democrats did [S4].
The bill received no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Uninsured Americans were better off: the coverage expansions and consumer protections the bill would have frozen stayed on schedule. Employers and higher-income taxpayers who would have gained from a delay got nothing from the bill's failure.

for.name: Rep. Tom Graves
for.what_they_did: Joined in introducing the bill at its introduction.

against.name: House committee leadership across eight committees
against.role: Chairs of Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, Natural Resources, Judiciary, Rules, Appropriations, and House Administration
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it in any committee.

against.name: President Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: Signed the ACA into law and opposed Republican efforts to delay or repeal it.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill never came to a floor vote where Democratic opposition would have been recorded.

industries.industry: Uninsured consumers awaiting the ACA's 2014 coverage expansions
industries.note: The bill would have indefinitely delayed the Medicaid expansion, premium subsidies, and the ban on pre-existing-condition denials for the millions of people those provisions cover. No preparation for implementation would have been allowed during the wait [S2] [S3].

industries.industry: Large employers subject to the employer coverage requirement
industries.note: A delay suspends the employer coverage requirement that had not yet taken effect, giving affected employers an open-ended reprieve from a cost the law would have imposed [S3].

Insurers would have been spared remaining regulatory deadlines during the freeze, but they had already built products, rate filings, and compliance systems around the law's schedule, and an indefinite freeze would have left that investment in limbo. The mandate and subsidies at stake in the pending cases are also what would bring insurers new customers [S3].

industries.industry: Higher-income taxpayers funding the law's subsidies
industries.note: Delaying the law's remaining provisions delays the taxes and revenue measures that fund its coverage expansions, a benefit concentrated among higher-income households [S3].
